summary: Describes how to benchmark devices that forward MPLS packets, covering the most common forwarding scenarios and delay measurements for IP flows. It builds on earlier benchmarking work such as RFC 2544 and RFC 1242. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: To compare how fast different mail sorters work, you need the same fair test for each. This document gives that test for routers that forward packets using labels.

subtitle: Standard tests for measuring MPLS router forwarding performance.

tldr.problem: Vendors need a fair and consistent way to measure how fast their MPLS routers forward packets, but existing benchmarking methods do not adequately cover MPLS-specific operations like label pushing, swapping, and popping.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines standardized test setups, frame formats, frame sizes, and measurements for throughput, latency, and frame loss across the five main MPLS forwarding scenarios, extending RFC 2544 methodology to MPLS.
tldr.outcome: This methodology allows vendors and operators to consistently benchmark MPLS forwarding devices under controlled conditions, enabling fair comparisons of equipment performance.

facts.label: Frame size increase for MPLS
facts.value: 4 octets per label in the stack

today: RFC 5695 provides the standard methodology for MPLS benchmarking and is used by vendors and operators to fairly evaluate MPLS forwarding device performance. It has become the reference standard for MPLS equipment testing in laboratories and vendor specifications.

sections.title: MPLS Forwarding and Benchmarking
sections.content: MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) is a forwarding architecture that routes packets based on short labels rather than IP addresses alone. Unlike simple IP forwarding, MPLS routers perform distinct operations: label push (adding a label when entering a labeled path), label swap (changing one label to another while forwarding), and label pop (removing a label when exiting a labeled path). These different operations place different loads on router hardware and create different performance profiles. Existing benchmarking methods like RFC 2544 do not address MPLS specifics. This document extends benchmarking methodology to cover MPLS, enabling fair performance comparisons of MPLS forwarding devices.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS routers do special tricks with packet labels. The old test doesn't measure those tricks, so this document adds tests just for them.

sections.title: Test Topology and Frame Formats
sections.content: The benchmarking topology consists of a Device Under Test (DUT) connected to a test tool with transmit (A) and receive (B) modules on both sides. Traffic is sent from test ports on the A modules, forwarded through the DUT, and received on the B modules. MPLS packets differ from IP packets in that they contain a label stack immediately after the Layer 2 header and before the IP payload. The methodology prescribes using IP packets as the MPLS payload because IP Prefix Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs) are fundamental to every MPLS network. Frame sizes must account for the addition of the MPLS label stack: a 4-octet label adds to the effective frame size, so MPLS test frame sizes are 4 octets larger than equivalent IP frame sizes. For example, while IP frames of 64 to 1518 octets are tested on Ethernet, MPLS frames of 68 to 1522 octets are tested to account for the label header.
sections.plainLanguage: You send packages through the router using special labeled containers. These containers are 4 bytes bigger than regular packages, so you need to test with bigger sizes.

sections.title: MPLS Forwarding Operations and Throughput Tests
sections.content: The methodology defines five core MPLS forwarding operations. Label Push converts an unlabeled IP packet into an MPLS packet by prepending a label; the test tool sends IP frames and expects to receive MPLS frames. Label Swap exchanges one MPLS label for another while forwarding; the test tool sends and receives MPLS frames with different labels. Label Pop (Unlabeled) removes the label, converting an MPLS packet back to IP; the test tool sends MPLS frames and receives IP frames. Label Pop (Aggregate) performs label pop and IP lookup on an aggregated prefix, then sends the result as IP. PHP (Penultimate Hop Popping) removes the label at the last hop before the destination using a reserved label value. For each operation, the methodology prescribes the test setup, frame formats, and procedure. Throughput is determined by finding the maximum offered load at which zero frames are dropped, using an iterative search algorithm. Results must report throughput in frames per second and bits per second for each tested frame size.
sections.plainLanguage: Five different tricks a router does: add a label, swap labels, remove a label, remove and look up, or have the second-to-last router remove it. Test each one with different size packages.

sections.title: Latency, Loss, and Recovery Measurements
sections.content: Beyond throughput, the methodology covers latency (the time the DUT takes to forward an MPLS packet), frame-loss rate (the percentage of frames not forwarded under overload), system recovery (how quickly a DUT bounces back after becoming overloaded), and reset procedures (how quickly the DUT recovers from a device or software reset). Each measurement reuses the test setups defined for the five forwarding operations, ensuring consistency. Trial duration depends on the routing protocols used: at least 30 seconds for static routing and at least 200 seconds for dynamic routing protocols to ensure the DUT maintains a stable control plane under stress. All sent traffic must be accounted for—the test tool verifies that the MPLS label stack is present, the label values are correct, and frames arrive on the correct ports with valid Frame Check Sequences.
sections.plainLanguage: Measure how fast packets get through, how many get lost when it's busy, and how quick the router recovers when it's overloaded.

sections.title: Test Configuration and Reporting
sections.content: The test methodology requires that all protocols and configurations be pre-established before test traffic starts. Dynamic protocols like LDP (Label Distribution Protocol), RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol with Traffic Engineering), and BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) must be running and have exchanged state, so the control plane is stable when testing begins. Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) must be disabled to ensure deterministic behavior. The test tool must configure port media MTU to accommodate the increased frame size from MPLS labels. Results must report numerous parameters: the FEC type (IPv4 or IPv6), label distribution protocol used, MPLS forwarding operation type, Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP), throughput metrics, port media, port speed, interface encapsulation, frame size, and number of port pairs. Test setups must disable non-essential features like Flow Control, QoS, and Graceful Restart unless explicitly tested.
sections.plainLanguage: Get all the protocols talking before you start. Write down everything about the test—what protocol, what size packages, which router ports—so another tester can repeat it.
